what_it_does: This paper addresses a class of computing systems called intermittent systems — tiny devices (like wireless sensors or implants) that run on harvested energy (from light, radio waves, or heat) and therefore power on and off unpredictably. Because the device may lose power at any moment, it must save its work-in-progress to a small non-volatile memory (storage that survives power loss) so it can pick up where it left off. The problem is that existing theoretical models of how these systems behave do not accurately reflect what actually happens at the hardware level when the energy reservoir is very small, leading engineers to design checkpoint-saving mechanisms that waste power or behave unsafely. This paper proposes a more accurate model of what happens during power interruptions on small-energy devices, and derives concrete design guidelines for both pre-planned (static) and adaptive (dynamic) checkpoint strategies that account for the real hardware constraints. The contribution is primarily conceptual and analytical rather than a new chip design.
